description: We are Team ASTERIA: three 12–13-year-old innovators from Dubai, UAE, and proud NASA Space Apps Global Alumni 2025. Skilled in Python, Java, AI, and Machine Learning, we blend creativity, curiosity, and teamwork to turn bold ideas into tech-driven solutions. ASTERIA (Astronomical SPHEREx Time-series Extraction & Rapid Image Analysis) helps anyone spot comets, asteroids, and new worlds moving across the sky. Explore ASTERIA and watch the sky move. 🌌
summary:
ASTERIA is an interactive web dashboard that makes NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey easy for anyone to explore. Since 2025, SPHEREx has mapped the entire sky every six months in 102 near-infrared bands, capturing over a billion objects. Finding what moves or changes in that data is hard for non-experts and usually means juggling several separate tools.

We built ASTERIA to bring SPHEREx observation data, Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD catalog overlays, an interactive time-series timeline, and an AI research assistant into one view. Users can search a target or coordinates, step through observation dates, compare images, and click any source to see its measurements, spectral features, and data limits. 

This matters because discoveries of comets, asteroids, and new worlds depend on noticing small shifts across huge image sets. ASTERIA helps students, educators, and researchers spot them quickly, and its AI answers stay grounded in the data on screen.
details:
ASTERIA is a research dashboard that turns NASA SPHEREx all-sky infrared data into visual exploration, so anyone can spot objects that move or change over time. Traditionally, exploring multi-epoch observations means cross-referencing separate catalogs, downloading heavy FITS files, and writing custom scripts. ASTERIA brings search, sky plotting, catalog comparison, and AI-guided analysis into a single view.


How it works:
Users search for a target or survey field (such as the COSMOS field) or enter coordinates (RA/Dec). ASTERIA plots SPHEREx observations alongside Gaia DR3 sources (stars, galaxy candidates, quasar candidates) and SIMBAD records on an interactive sky map. Users can scrub through observation dates on a playback timeline, click any source to see its magnitudes, parallax distance, classifier probabilities, and spectral features such as ice signatures, and ask an integrated AI assistant questions grounded in the data on screen. [Comet Chaser mode follows a moving target, such as comet 3I/ATLAS, across SPHEREx images using JPL Horizons positions, showing its path and how its spectrum changes.]


Key Benefits & Impact:

  • Fewer tools switching: target search, multi-catalog comparison, observation metadata, and research discussion in one workspace.
  • Empowers students & educators: Makes sky coordinates, source classifications, and multi-epoch observations easy to explore hands-on.
  • Supports initial research: Helps enthusiasts and researchers inspect nearby sources, spot missing measurements, and form hypotheses quickly.

Tools & Technologies:

  • Frontend & Visualization: HTML/CSS, Tailwind CSS, React / Next.js with interactive sky plotting (MapLibre / Deck.gl / Three.js)
  • Backend & Processing: Python (FastAPI, NumPy, Astropy, OpenCV) and JavaScript for data retrieval, alignment, and difference detection which subtracts one aligned image from another so moving or changing objects stand out
  • Data Visualization: Matplotlib and custom interactive sky plot overlays
  • AI & Development Assistants: ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude, GitHub Copilot

Creative Elements:

  • Unified Multi-Catalog Sky Plot: Visually distinguishes SPHEREx observations, Gaia DR3 stars, galaxies, quasars, and SIMBAD objects on a single interactive coordinate grid.
  • Interactive Observation Timeline: Lets users step or play through SPHEREx observation epochs to track changes over time.
  • Context-Aware Research Chat: Keeps the selected sky field and source telemetry in view while users ask follow-up questions about terminology, source types, and spectral features.
  • Transparent Data Reporting: Clearly flags unavailable parallax distances or catalog timeouts so users understand measurement boundaries.
